explanations.answer: To go around the land of Edom
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The text says they set out from Mount Hor along the route to the Red Sea "…in order to bypass the land of Edom." So the passage gives us the reason for the route, and that's your answer. I've taken the long way around my own kitchen to dodge a pan I burned, so I get it.

Elim is a place from earlier in Israel's journey (Exodus 15:27), and it isn't what this verse is about. Here the text says they set out from Mount Hor along the route to the Red Sea, in order to bypass the land of Edom. The detour was about getting around Edom. I've picked the wrong oven setting plenty of times myself, so no worries.

Jethro is the priest of Midian and Moses' father-in-law (Exodus 3:1). He's a real name from Moses' story, but he isn't in this passage. The text says they were going the long way "…in order to bypass the land of Edom." That's the whole reason given. Good guess for a name that sounds like it belongs, friend.

Yes, baker. The text says the people "…grew impatient on the journey". Their patience ran out somewhere along the way. I know that feeling. I once got antsy waiting for a batch to cool, and that's a ten minute wait.

Not quite, friend. The text says plainly that "…the people grew impatient on the journey" (Numbers 21:4). So the statement is True. The impatience is where this whole story starts, and the next verse shows what it turns into.

That's right. The people "…spoke against God and against Moses…" and Moses is Israel's leader. So the complaint went to God and to the man leading them. I think that's a tough spot to stand in, and I bet Moses felt it.

Aaron is Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), but this verse doesn't mention him. The text says the people "…spoke against God and against Moses…" The blank is Moses. It's an easy name to grab, friend, since Aaron is a name you meet around Moses.

Joshua was Moses' attendant (Exodus 24:13), but he isn't named in this verse. Here the people "…spoke against God and against Moses…" So Moses fills the blank. Good try, friend. Joshua's a name worth knowing, but he's not in this complaint.
Right, baker. They say, "There is no bread or water…" That's the complaint, word for word. I'll just say it: a kitchen with no bread or water would make even me grumpy.

Shade and shelter sound like real wilderness problems, but they aren't what the people say here. Their words are, "There is no bread or water, and we detest this wretched food!" The complaint is about what they have to eat and drink. Easy mix-up, friend.

Tents and blankets make sense for a camp, but the people don't mention them. What they say is, "There is no bread or water, and we detest this wretched food!" Their complaint is about food and water. I'd have guessed blankets too on a cold night, I'll admit.

Yes, baker. The text says, "…the LORD sent venomous snakes among the people, and many of the Israelites were bitten and died." This is the heavy turn in the story. It's a serious moment, and the next verses show where it goes.

Locusts are in the Bible, as one of the plagues on Egypt (Exodus 10:13), but not here. This passage says, "…the LORD sent venomous snakes among the people…" It's a good guess from a different part of the story, friend.

Hail is another one from Egypt's plagues (Exodus 9:23), so I see where your mind went. Here, though, the text says, "…the LORD sent venomous snakes among the people…" Snakes are the answer this time. Hail belongs to a different story, baker.

That's it, baker. They tell Moses, "We have sinned by speaking against the LORD and against you." They said it out loud and named it. That's not an easy thing to do, and I've had to do it more than once myself.

They did suffer, since many were bitten and died. But that isn't the word they use. They say, "We have sinned by speaking against the LORD and against you." They own what they did, and that's the word for the blank, friend.

I can see why "lost" feels right out in a wilderness. But the people don't say it. They say, "We have sinned by speaking against the LORD and against you." They name what they did, baker, and that's what goes in the blank.

explanations.answer: Intercede so the LORD takes the snakes away
explanations.explanation: Exactly right. They say, "Intercede with the LORD so He will take the snakes away from us." To intercede is to speak to God for someone else. They asked Moses to be that voice, and the text says, "So Moses interceded for the people."

explanations.answer: Lead them back down to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt does come up in their complaint, when they say "Why have you led us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness?" (Numbers 21:5). But the request they bring to Moses is different: "Intercede with the LORD so He will take the snakes away from us." The ask is about the snakes, friend.

explanations.answer: Build a wall around the camp
explanations.explanation: A wall sounds like a sensible fix against snakes, I'll give you that. But the people never ask for one. They ask Moses, "Intercede with the LORD so He will take the snakes away from us." They looked to the LORD for the answer, baker.

Yes, baker. The LORD tells Moses, "Make a fiery serpent and mount it on a pole." Picture Moses hearing that one. I bet he had questions, and I'd have had a whole list. But the text says he did it: he made a bronze snake and mounted it on a pole (Numbers 21:9).

A golden lampstand is a real item in the Bible (Exodus 25:31), but it isn't what the LORD asks for here. He says, "Make a fiery serpent and mount it on a pole." The pole is the clue, friend. A lampstand would've been a lot less scary to carve.

Silver trumpets do show up in Numbers (Numbers 10:2), so you're in the right book, baker. But here the LORD says, "Make a fiery serpent and mount it on a pole." The trumpets were for a different job, and this one needed a serpent.
That's right. The LORD says, "When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live." Looking is the whole thing, baker. Just look, and live.
People do bow in the Bible, like in Exodus 4:31, but bowing isn't the word here. The LORD says, "When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live." The word is looks, friend. No bowing needed.

Pointing would be a handy move when you're panicking about a snake. But the LORD's words are, "When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live." The blank is looks. Points at the pole doesn't make the cut, baker.

Not this time, friend. The text says, "If anyone who was bitten looked at the bronze snake, he would live." That's anyone, and it's not limited to the first one. So the statement is False. There's no race here, and no prize for being first.

Right, baker. The text says, "If anyone who was bitten looked at the bronze snake, he would live." It says anyone, not just the first person. Every bitten person who looked would live, and there was no line to stand in or number to take.
